I study how small open economies — particularly Taiwan — design industrial and trade
policy under geopolitical pressure. My current work spans two empirical projects: a
cross-national analysis of how security salience shapes trade restrictions on geopolitical
rivals' goods, with Taiwan's EV ban as the crucial case; and a study of VAT pass-through
in Philippine pharmaceutical markets, where procurement regulation suppresses the consumer
welfare gains from fiscal reform. A third project examines how Taiwanese SMEs adjust
supply chains and export markets under sustained geopolitical disruption. I combine
quantitative methods with Mandarin-language primary source access — MOEA firm data, SMEA
surveys, Legislative Yuan records — that most researchers working on these questions
cannot use directly.

Currently: MPA/ID Candidate 2027, Harvard Kennedy School. Consultant (Intern), African
Development Bank — Africa Legal Support Facility (ALSF), Jun–Sep 2026. Former Economics
Intern, Philippine Competition Commission, Economics Office.

## Featured Research

### The Security Premium: Why Taiwan Maintains the World's Most Restrictive Policy toward Chinese Electric Vehicles

**Authors:** Sally Tsai · Cheng Wang · Luis Hong Sanchez
**Venue:** Harvard Kennedy School, DPI-410: The Politics of Development · Spring 2026

**Methods:** Cross-national ordered logit (N=48) · Synthetic control · Within-case
process trace · Leave-one-out cross-validation · Placebo inference

Taiwan produces 275,000 vehicles annually, hosts no domestically owned EV brand, and
has no organized producer lobby — the Grossman-Helpman model predicts minimal trade
restriction. Its observed policy is a complete ban on Chinese vehicles, the most
restrictive of any economy in the world. We argue the missing variable is *security
salience*: when the import source is a geopolitical adversary capable of weaponizing
economic interdependence, governments apply a security premium above the
Grossman-Helpman equilibrium.

Three methods triangulate on this conclusion. A cross-national ordered logit across
60+ countries shows Taiwan is the largest positive residual in the industry-only model;
when the EU is correctly treated as a single policy decision-maker, the security channel
achieves statistical significance (α = −0.524, SE = 0.231, p<0.05). A leave-one-out
cross-validation estimates only a 4% probability that Taiwan would receive maximum
restriction absent the security channel. A synthetic control places Taiwan's vehicle
production 29% below its counterfactual trajectory after 2016. A within-case process
trace provides mechanism identification: policy tightening began only when the DPP
raised security salience after 2016 — the same structural threat under the KMT from
2008–2016 produced no additional restriction, isolating political salience as the
operative variable rather than structural threat level.

The paper introduces a 2×2 framework (ICE industry size × EV adoption level) that
generates quadrant-specific predictions for 193 countries, identifying where the
Grossman-Helpman channel dominates, where the security channel is necessary and
sufficient, and where consumer welfare overwhelms both. Taiwan in Q3 (small ICE
industry, low EV adoption, maximum restriction) is the cleanest test case for the
security premium.

**Policy implication:** As Chinese EV manufacturers expand globally, the
security-augmented model predicts the frontier of trade restriction will be determined
by security alignment, not domestic industry size.

[View paper →](pdfs/tsai-wang-sanchez-security-premium-2026.pdf)

### VAT Pass-Through in Philippine Pharmaceutical Markets: Evidence from the TRAIN Act

**Authors:** Sally Tsai · Carlos Vega
**Affiliations:** Harvard Kennedy School; Philippine Competition Commission /
Centre for Competition Policy, University of East Anglia · June 2026

**Methods:** Difference-in-differences (product FE, 8 pre-treatment quarters, event
study) · Triple-difference by license type · Synthetic control (ASEAN comparators) ·
Parallel quantity DiD

The 2019 TRAIN Act (RA 10963) exempted essential medicines for hypertension, diabetes,
and high cholesterol from the Philippines' 12% value-added tax — a reform explicitly
designed to lower out-of-pocket drug costs for Filipino households. Using product-level
quarterly IQVIA MIDAS data (2009–2021, N=44,339 observations, 1,953 products), we find
*no pass-through to patients*: treated drug prices rose approximately 2.3% relative to
controls following the exemption (β̂ = 0.023\*\*\*, SE = 0.005), with firms absorbing the
tax relief entirely as margin expansion on unregulated low-volume products. Volume-weighted
estimates are statistically indistinguishable from zero, consistent with procurement
regulation suppressing pass-through for the high-volume products that dominate patient
spending.

A triple-difference decomposition by license type reveals the competitive mechanism.
Originators with inelastic brand-loyal demand extracted the full tax relief as margin
(β̂\_O = 0.045\*\*\*); branded non-originators showed a significantly smaller response
(β̂\_B = 0.013\*\*); unbranded generics facing price competition showed no significant
adjustment (β̂\_U = 0.002, n.s.). Wald tests confirm the originator–generic gradient is
statistically distinct (p<0.001). A parallel DiD on quantities finds retail volumes of
treated drugs fell approximately 20% (β̂ = −0.208\*\*\*, SE = 0.063) while hospital
volumes were unchanged — a *double welfare loss* in the retail channel: list prices rose
and retail consumption fell simultaneously. Back-of-envelope welfare accounting finds
Filipino households incurred roughly PHP 216–262 more in annual essential drug costs
than they would have saved under full pass-through — approximately 4–5% of baseline
out-of-pocket spending.

**Policy implication:** VAT exemptions are an ineffective instrument for reducing
patient drug costs when procurement regulation already binds for high-volume products.
The fiscal cost accrues to producers, not patients.

[View paper →](pdfs/tsai-vega-vat-passthrough-2026.pdf)

## Research in Progress

**SME Trade Adjustment under Geopolitical Pressure** *(SYPA — in progress)*

How do Taiwanese SMEs adjust export destinations and supply chains under sustained
geopolitical pressure from China? Identification exploits three distinct escalation
episodes — the 2016 DPP election, 2019–20 trade tensions, and the 2022 Pelosi visit
and PLA exercises — as temporal variation in treatment intensity, using staggered DiD
(Callaway-Sant'Anna) on MOEA Industry Statistics and SMEA Annual Survey firm data.
New Southbound Policy subsidies provide a natural treatment-control comparison for
identifying intentional diversification responses versus passive adjustment.
